items.title: Joe Wilder Part 2 interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, October 12, 1998
items.q: we used to listen to Horace Heidt and those bands

ctx.x: Do you recall if your parents listened to the music that you liked and how did they feel about it? Did they feel that —

My father, being a musician, is the one that pointed me I guess in the right direction, and my mother too for that matter. But my father used to listen, we had the radio and that’s all you had, and you listened to the old bands, some of which people wonder where I’m coming from with this, but there were bands like Gus Anheim, Paul Whiteman of course and Duke Ellington was one of my father’s favorites, and there was Cab Calloway and Fletcher Henderson and all these different bands, and then we used to listen to…
Yeah. He even liked the syrupy stuff.

items.title: Joe Wilder — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: We did the ABC Dance Party, where we imitated all the bands, Horace Heidt, Glen Gray, Count Basie, Duke Ellington.

ctx.x: Why was that? What made him a good . . . ?

He set a certain tone there. Everybody deported himself in a very dignified manner. The people who ran the American Broadcasting Company were highly respectful of him, and consequently they treated the musicians with great respect, and he, in turn, demanded that the musicians respect the job and so forth. It was fantastic. We were doing the Metropolitan Opera Auditions of the Air. I – at that point I was doing – I was the substitute trumpet player. Whenever they needed somebody, they would call me. You did…
played second trumpet in the brass quintet with – Ray Crisara was the first trumpet player. We did things like that.
